hook: Some regions are awkward to slice top to bottom. A pond whose banks are a parabola opening sideways and a straight wall has a bottom edge that switches curves halfway across. Turn your knife sideways: every horizontal strip runs from the same left bank to the same right bank, and one integral does the job.

prereq.why: Take the cube root of both sides: $x = \sqrt[3]{y} = y^{1/3}$. This is the inverse function.

prereq.q: Where does the parabola $y = 6 - x^2$ meet the line $y = x$?

figure.caption: A horizontal strip between $x = y^2$ and $x = y + 2$: its length is right minus left, and the limits are $y$-values.

chain.cause: Write each edge of the region as $x$ in terms of $y$
chain.effect: a horizontal strip at height $y$ runs from $x_{\text{left}}(y)$ to $x_{\text{right}}(y)$

chain.cause: The strip has length right minus left and thickness $\Delta y$
Stack the strips from the bottom of the region to the top

chain.effect: the limits $c$ and $d$ are the $y$-values where the region starts and ends

ideas: Integrating with respect to $y$: area $= \int_c^d \left(x_{\text{right}}(y) - x_{\text{left}}(y)\right)\,dy$, right minus left.
Rewrite each curve as $x = $ (something in $y$) first: $y = \sqrt{x}$ becomes $x = y^2$, $y = \ln x$ becomes $x = e^y$.
Limits are $y$-values. Find them by setting the two $x$-expressions equal and solving for $y$.
Choose $y$ when each side edge is one formula but the top or bottom edge changes partway across; slicing in $x$ would take two integrals.
Both ways give the same area when done correctly.

misconception.wrong: For an integral in $dy$, you can keep the $x$-values of the crossing points as the limits.
misconception.right: The limits belong to the variable of integration. With $dy$, use the $y$-coordinates of the crossings: for $x = y^2$ and $x = y + 2$ that is $y = -1$ to $y = 2$, not $x = 1$ to $x = 4$.

summary: When a region is easier to cut sideways, write its edges as $x$ in terms of $y$ and integrate right minus left from the lowest $y$ to the highest: $A = \int_c^d \left(x_{\text{right}} - x_{\text{left}}\right)\,dy$. The limits are $y$-values, found by setting the two edges equal.

connections.label: Back: area with functions of x (8.4)
